# Categorical data and the Dirichlet distribution

## From two categories to many

::: {#def-categorical-and-multinomial-models .definition}
## Categorical and multinomial models

For two categories, a Bernoulli trial has probabilities $(p,1-p)$ and an aggregated count has a binomial distribution. For $K$ categories, let 

$$
 \pvec=(p_1,\ldots,p_K)^{\mathsf T},
 \qquad p_k\geq0,
 \qquad \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1.
$$


 A single observation $Y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$ has 

$$
 \Pr(Y_i=k\given\pvec)=p_k.
$$


 For $n$ conditionally independent observations define 

$$
 X_k=\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}\{Y_i=k\}.
$$


 Then $\sum_kX_k=n$ and 

$$
 \xvec\given\pvec\sim\Mult(n,\pvec).
$$


:::

To derive its mass function, first choose which $x_1$ positions receive category 1, then which $x_2$ of the remaining positions receive category 2, and so on: \begin{align*}
 \binom{n}{x_1}
 \binom{n-x_1}{x_2}\cdots
 \binom{x_{K-1}+x_K}{x_{K-1}}
 &=\frac{n!}{x_1!(n-x_1)!}
   \frac{(n-x_1)!}{x_2!(n-x_1-x_2)!}\cdots\\
 &=\frac{n!}{x_1!\cdots x_K!}.
\end{align*} Every one of those sequences has probability $\prod_kp_k^{x_k}$, so \begin{equation}
 p(\xvec\given\pvec)
 =\frac{n!}{\prod_{k=1}^Kx_k!}
  \prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{x_k}.
 \label{eq:multinomial-pmf-book}
\end{equation} As a likelihood in $\pvec$, 

$$
 L(\pvec;\xvec)\propto\prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{x_k}.
$$


## The Dirichlet prior

::: {#def-dirichlet-distribution .definition}
## Dirichlet distribution

The conjugate prior for $\pvec$ is the Dirichlet distribution. Write 

$$
 \alpha_0=\sum_{k=1}^K\alpha_k,
 \qquad \alpha_k>0.
$$


 The multivariate Beta function is 

$$
 B(\vect\alpha)
 =\frac{\prod_{k=1}^K\Gamma(\alpha_k)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_0)}.
$$


 Then \begin{equation}
 p(\pvec\given\vect\alpha)
 =\frac1{B(\vect\alpha)}
   \prod_{k=1}^Kp_k^{\alpha_k-1},
 \qquad \pvec\in\mathcal S_{K-1},
 \label{eq:dirichlet-density-book}
\end{equation} where 

$$
 \mathcal S_{K-1}
 =\left\{\pvec:p_k\geq0,\ \sum_{k=1}^Kp_k=1\right\}
$$


 is the probability simplex.

:::

::: {#prp-the-beta-distribution-is-the-two-category-dirichlet .proposition}
## The Beta distribution is the two-category Dirichlet

When $K=2$, write $p_1=p$ and $p_2=1-p$. Restricting the Dirichlet density to the one-dimensional simplex gives 

$$
 p(p\given\alpha_1,\alpha_2)
 =\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_1+\alpha_2)}
        {\Gamma(\alpha_1)\Gamma(\alpha_2)}
   p^{\alpha_1-1}(1-p)^{\alpha_2-1},
$$


 which is exactly $\BetaDist(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)$. The Dirichlet is therefore a genuine extension of the Beta family rather than merely a similar-looking density.

:::

The prior cannot itself be multinomial. A multinomial distribution is a discrete distribution for a vector of counts, whereas the unknown $\pvec$ varies continuously over the simplex. The likelihood may be discrete in the data while the prior and posterior are continuous in the parameter; these are different arguments of the same Bayesian calculation.

For $K=3$ the simplex is a triangle. Beginning with three categories and a triangle is easier than beginning with the general simplex, although the triangle eventually has to give way.

![The three-category probability simplex.](../figures/part1-inline-simplex.pdf){#fig-inline-simplex}

If all $\alpha_k=1$, the density in \eqref{eq:dirichlet-density-book} is constant on the simplex. This means uniform density over valid probability vectors. It does not force $p_1=\cdots=p_K=1/K$.

For the Dirichlet distribution, separate location from concentration. The ratios $\alpha_k/\alpha_0$ describe the centre of the prior, while $\alpha_0=\sum_k\alpha_k$ controls how tightly probability vectors cluster around it. Multiplying every $\alpha_k$ by the same constant keeps the centre but changes the strength of the prior. That is a more useful way to reason about these parameters than trying to picture a high-dimensional density one coordinate at a time.

When every $\alpha_k<1$, the density favours sparse probability vectors near the boundary. For $\alpha_1=\cdots=\alpha_K=0.1$, typical draws put most of their mass on one category: a "winner takes all" prior. The density is singular along the boundary, so the careful statement is about the distribution of draws, not a finite interior mode located at a corner.

![Draws from three symmetric Dirichlet distributions. The uniform $\Dir(1,1,1)$ fills the triangle; increasing the common concentration to $5$ pulls probability vectors toward $(1/3,1/3,1/3)$; reducing it to $0.1$ puts most draws near an edge or corner. Symmetry fixes the same centre in all three panels, so the visible change is concentration rather than location.](../figures/part1-fig-05-dirichlet-simplex.pdf){#fig-05-dirichlet-simplex}

One should be prepared to abandon a visualisation that is not helping.

::: {#prp-multinomial-central-limit-theorem .proposition}
## Multinomial central limit theorem

Let $\xvec\sim\Mult(n,\pvec)$ and $\widehat\pvec=\xvec/n$. For fixed interior $\pvec$, define the covariance matrix 

$$
 \mat{\Sigma}(\pvec)
 =\operatorname{diag}(\pvec)-\pvec\pvec^{\mathsf T}.
$$


 Then 

$$
 \sqrt n\,(\widehat\pvec-\pvec)
 \xrightarrow{\mathcal D}
 \Normal_K\!\left(
  \vect 0,
  \mat{\Sigma}(\pvec)
 \right).
$$


 The covariance matrix is singular because the components of $\widehat\pvec-\pvec$ sum to zero. On the $(K-1)$-dimensional simplex, the count cloud therefore tightens at the usual $n^{-1/2}$ rate and becomes locally normal.

:::

## Moments and the mode

::: {#prp-dirichlet-moments .proposition}
## Dirichlet moments

Standard Dirichlet integrals give \begin{align*}
 \E(P_k)&=\frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_0},\\
 \E(P_k^2)&=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_k+1)}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\\
 \E(P_jP_k)&=\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}
                  {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)},\qquad j\neq k.
\end{align*}

:::

Therefore \begin{align*}
 \Var(P_k)
 &=\E(P_k^2)-\E(P_k)^2\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_k+1)}
          {\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)}
   -\frac{\alpha_k^2}{\alpha_0^2}\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_k\alpha_0(\alpha_k+1)
          -\alpha_k^2(\alpha_0+1)}
         {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)}\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_k(\alpha_0-\alpha_k)}
         {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)},\\[4pt]
 \Cov(P_j,P_k)
 &=\E(P_jP_k)-\E(P_j)\E(P_k)\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}{\alpha_0(\alpha_0+1)}
   -\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}{\alpha_0^2}\\
 &=-\frac{\alpha_j\alpha_k}
          {\alpha_0^2(\alpha_0+1)}.
\end{align*} The negative covariance is forced by the sum-to-one constraint.

To derive the interior mode, maximise 

$$
 \ell(\pvec)=\sum_{k=1}^K(\alpha_k-1)\log p_k
$$


 subject to $\sum_kp_k=1$. The Lagrangian is 

$$
 \mathcal L(\pvec,\lambda)
 =\sum_{k=1}^K(\alpha_k-1)\log p_k
  +\lambda\left(\sum_{k=1}^Kp_k-1\right).
$$


 Differentiating, 

$$
 \frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial p_k}
 =\frac{\alpha_k-1}{p_k}+\lambda=0
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 p_k=-\frac{\alpha_k-1}{\lambda}.
$$


 Summing over $k$ and imposing the constraint gives 

$$
 1=\sum_kp_k
 =-\frac1\lambda\sum_k(\alpha_k-1)
 =-\frac{\alpha_0-K}{\lambda},
$$


 so $\lambda=-(\alpha_0-K)$.

::: {#prp-interior-dirichlet-mode .proposition}
## Interior Dirichlet mode

Consequently, \begin{equation}
 \operatorname{mode}(P_k)
 =\frac{\alpha_k-1}{\alpha_0-K}.
 \label{eq:dir-mode-book}
\end{equation} This derivation requires every $\alpha_k>1$. Otherwise the mode may lie on a face or corner of the simplex.

:::

## Dirichlet--Multinomial conjugacy

Multiply the fully normalised likelihood and prior: \begin{align*}
 p(\xvec\given\pvec)p(\pvec)
 &=\frac{n!}{\prod_kx_k!}
   \prod_kp_k^{x_k}
   \frac1{B(\vect\alpha)}
   \prod_kp_k^{\alpha_k-1}\\
 &=\frac{n!}{\prod_kx_k!B(\vect\alpha)}
   \prod_kp_k^{x_k+\alpha_k-1}.
\end{align*} The integral over the simplex of the product is $B(\vect\alpha+\xvec)$, so \begin{align*}
 p(\xvec)
 &=\frac{n!}{\prod_kx_k!}
   \frac{B(\vect\alpha+\xvec)}
        {B(\vect\alpha)}\\
 &=\frac{n!}{\prod_kx_k!}
   \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_0)}{\Gamma(\alpha_0+n)}
   \prod_{k=1}^K
   \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_k+x_k)}{\Gamma(\alpha_k)}.
 \label{eq:dir-mult-evidence-book}
\end{align*}

::: {#thm-dirichlet-multinomial-conjugacy .theorem}
## Dirichlet--Multinomial conjugacy

After division by this evidence, \begin{equation}
 \boxed{
 \pvec\given\xvec
 \sim\Dir(\alpha_1+x_1,\ldots,\alpha_K+x_K)}.
 \label{eq:dir-mult-post-book}
\end{equation}

:::

The posterior mean is \begin{align*}
 \E(P_k\given\xvec)
 &=\frac{\alpha_k+x_k}{\alpha_0+n}\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_0}{\alpha_0+n}
    \frac{\alpha_k}{\alpha_0}
  +\frac n{\alpha_0+n}\frac{x_k}{n}.
\end{align*} The posterior mode, when every $\alpha_k+x_k>1$, is 

$$
 \widehat p_{k,\mathrm{MAP}}
 =\frac{x_k+\alpha_k-1}{n+\alpha_0-K}.
$$


 Thus $\alpha_k$ behaves like a pseudo-count for the mean and $\alpha_k-1$ for the mode.

For a new categorical observation, \begin{align*}
 \Pr(Y_{n+1}=k\given\xvec)
 &=\int\Pr(Y_{n+1}=k\given\pvec)
       p(\pvec\given\xvec)\dd\pvec\\
 &=\int p_kp(\pvec\given\xvec)\dd\pvec\\
 &=\E(P_k\given\xvec)\\
 &=\frac{\alpha_k+x_k}{\alpha_0+n}.
\end{align*}

## Advertising-response table

::: {#exm-advertising-responses .example}
## Advertising responses

The following table classifies $501$ people by gender and response to an advertising campaign:

|  | Negative | Neutral | Positive | Total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Male | 53 | 57 | 147 | 257 |
| Female | 93 | 38 | 113 | 244 |
| Total | 146 | 95 | 260 | 501 |

**Question.** Use an unrestricted six-cell multinomial with the uniform prior 

$$
 \pvec\sim\Dir(1,1,1,1,1,1).
$$


 Find the posterior distribution and the posterior mean and MAP estimate of the male-negative cell probability.

**Solution.** The conjugate update gives 

$$
 \pvec\given\xvec
 \sim\Dir(54,58,148,94,39,114).
$$


 For the male-negative cell, 

$$
 \E(P_{11}\given\xvec)=\frac{54}{501+6}=\frac{54}{507}
 \approx0.1065,
$$


 while 

$$
 \widehat p_{11,\mathrm{MAP}}
 =\frac{54-1}{507-6}=\frac{53}{501}
 \approx0.1058.
$$


 The MAP equals the maximum-likelihood cell proportion because every prior parameter equals one.

:::
## Exercises

::: {#exr-beta-hidden-inside-dirichlet .exercise}
## Beta hidden inside Dirichlet

Set $K=2$ in the Dirichlet normalising constant and substitute $p_2=1-p_1$. Recover the complete Beta density, including its normalising constant.

:::

::: {#exr-why-not-a-multinomial-prior .exercise}
## Why not a multinomial prior?

A student proposes a multinomial prior for $\pvec$. State the support and type of a multinomial random variable and of $\pvec$, then explain precisely why the proposal assigns probability to the wrong kind of object.

:::

::: {#exr-small-concentrations .exercise}
## Small concentrations

For $K=3$ compare $\Dir(1,1,1)$, $\Dir(5,5,5)$, and $\Dir(0.1,0.1,0.1)$. Give their common centre, compare their total concentrations, and describe where a typical draw lies. Why is "all categories are near zero" impossible?

:::

::: {#exr-the-simplex-clt .exercise}
## The simplex CLT

Starting from $\Cov(X_j,X_k)=-np_jp_k$ for $j\neq k$ and $\Var(X_k)=np_k(1-p_k)$, derive the covariance matrix of $\sqrt n(\widehat\pvec-\pvec)$. Show that multiplication by the all-ones vector gives zero.

:::

::: {#exr-dirichlet-updating .exercise}
## Dirichlet updating

Beginning with \eqref{eq:multinomial-pmf-book} and \eqref{eq:dirichlet-density-book}, retain every factor involving $\pvec$ and derive the posterior parameters. Then derive the posterior predictive probability that one new observation falls in category $k$.

:::

**Applied problems.**

::: {#ex-applied-restaurant .exercise}
## Restaurant ordering methods

A restaurant observed the following numbers of orders yesterday:

|  | Dine-in | Take-away | Pick-up | Delivery |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Count | 63 | 19 | 3 | 38 |

Let $\pvec=(p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)$ be the corresponding population proportions.

1.  With $\xvec\given\pvec\sim\Mult(123,\pvec)$ and $\pvec\sim\Dir(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_4)$, identify the posterior.

2.  Last week's percentages were $44.79\%$, $27.60\%$, $7.36\%$, and $20.25\%$. Explain how to use these proportions to choose the direction of $\vect\alpha$, and how a chosen total concentration records the weight given to last week.

3.  Using a prior equivalent, for posterior-mean purposes, to last week's proportions plus one baseline count in each category, report posterior means and equal-tailed $95\%$ credible intervals for $p_1$, $p_4$, $p_1+p_2+p_3$, and $p_1-p_4$.

[Solution](#sol-applied-restaurant)

:::
